children.label: Bucatini
children.fact: Its center hole helps sauce cling inside every strand.

children.label: Perciatelli
children.fact: In southern Italy, it is often treated as the rustic cousin of bucatini.

children.label: Bigoli
children.fact: A thick hollow pasta from Venice, traditionally made with whole wheat or duck eggs, and historically the pasta of the poor — served on days when meat was forbidden.

children.label: Spaghettoni
children.fact: It is thicker than spaghetti, so it keeps more bite in saucy dishes.

children.label: Spaghetti
children.fact: Its name means little strings, not noodles.

children.label: Vermicelli
children.fact: In Italy it is slightly thicker than spaghetti, the opposite of some export labels.

children.label: Spaghetti alla chitarra
children.fact: Made by pressing dough through a wooden frame strung with guitar wires — each strand has a square cross-section, not round, which holds sauce differently than regular spaghetti.

children.label: Pici
children.fact: A hand-rolled pasta from Tuscany, each strand rolled by hand into an uneven thick rope. No two pieces are identical, and that irregularity is considered the point.

children.label: Spaghettini
children.fact: It cooks fast enough that a distracted minute can ruin it.

children.label: Fedelini
children.fact: Older cookbooks called it the elegant soup pasta of Genoa.

children.label: Capellini
children.fact: Its name means little hairs, which is exactly how delicate it is.

children.label: Capellini d'angelo
children.fact: Angel-hair style strands can overcook in well under two minutes.

children.label: Filindeu
children.fact: One of the rarest pastas in Italy, it is pulled and folded into 256 fine threads, dried as a woven sheet, then broken into broth for a Sardinian pilgrimage feast.

children.label: Lasagne
children.fact: The plural name is traditional even when people mean one sheet.

children.label: Pappardelle
children.fact: Its name comes from a Tuscan verb meaning to gobble up.

children.label: Tagliatelle
children.fact: Bologna preserves an official golden model for its ideal width.

children.label: Fettuccine
children.fact: Its name means little ribbons, which is the whole design brief.

children.label: Scialatielli
children.fact: Invented in 1978 by a single chef in Amalfi — one of the few modern pastas with a known inventor and a documented birth date.

children.label: Tagliolini
children.fact: It is essentially a finer northern cousin of tagliatelle.

children.label: Linguine
children.fact: Its name means little tongues, which is why it sits between flat and round pasta.

children.label: Linguettine
children.fact: This slimmer linguine variant is prized for lighter seafood sauces.

children.label: Trenette
children.fact: In Liguria, the classic pesto plate is often trenette with potatoes and green beans mixed directly into the pasta, not served as sides.

children.label: Tajarin
children.fact: A Piedmontese ribbon made with an unusually egg-rich dough, traditionally so rich that old recipes call for dozens of yolks per kilo of flour.

children.label: Mafaldine
children.fact: Named after Princess Mafalda of Savoy — the ruffled edges were meant to resemble the lace trim of royal dresses.

children.label: Pizzoccheri
children.fact: Made with buckwheat flour from the Valtellina valley in Lombardy — one of the very few Italian pastas not made from wheat. Traditionally baked with cabbage, potato, and melted cheese.

children.label: Penne
children.fact: It is named after a quill pen because of the pointed diagonal ends.

children.label: Penne rigate
children.fact: Rigate simply means ridged, giving tomato sauce more grip.

children.label: Pennette
children.fact: It is the smaller penne you see in many quick weeknight bakes.

children.label: Rigatoni
children.fact: Its grooves were made for meaty sauces to lodge in every channel.

children.label: Tortiglioni
children.fact: Unlike rigatoni, the grooves twist around the tube in a spiral, so sauce winds through the pasta instead of sitting in straight channels.

children.label: Paccheri
children.fact: So large you can stuff individual tubes like small cannelloni. The name likely comes from a Neapolitan word for a slap — because of the slapping sound they make against the plate.

children.label: Calamarata
children.fact: Shaped to mimic rings of calamari — traditionally served with actual squid so the pasta and the seafood are visually indistinguishable on the plate.

children.label: Macaroni
children.fact: The elbow shape became standard later than the word itself.

children.label: Ziti
children.fact: Traditionally it was snapped by hand before going into baked dishes.

children.label: Mezze maniche
children.fact: Means "half sleeves" — a shorter, wider version of rigatoni. A Roman staple, almost always the pasta used in an authentic amatriciana.

children.label: Ditaloni
children.fact: A larger version of ditalini, the name means "big thimbles." The preferred pasta for pasta e fagioli in Naples — the thick tube traps beans inside it.

children.label: Fusilli
children.fact: The spiral was originally formed by wrapping dough around a spindle.

children.label: Spirali
children.fact: Many brands use this name for tighter corkscrews than classic fusilli.

children.label: Trofie
children.fact: The only pasta traditionally designed specifically for pesto — its tight twist and rough texture grip the sauce so well that Ligurians consider it almost a rule that trofie must be served with pesto genovese.

children.label: Gramigna
children.fact: In Bologna, gramigna is so closely tied to sausage that menus often list the pair together as if they were a single dish rather than pasta plus sauce.

children.label: Fusilli bucati
children.fact: It combines spiral grooves with a hollow center for double sauce capture.

children.label: Cavatappi
children.fact: Means "corkscrews" — a hollow spiral that combines the sauce-trapping of a tube with the grip of a twist. Invented in the 1970s and now one of the most copied shapes globally.

children.label: Farfalle
children.fact: Its name means butterflies, though many diners insist on bow ties.

children.label: Mandala / Rotelle
children.fact: Designed in the 1960s to mimic wagon wheels. Food engineers spent months perfecting the spoke-to-rim ratio so the whole piece cooks evenly — the spokes and rim are different thicknesses.

children.label: Farfalline
children.fact: These miniature butterflies often show up in brothy soups.

children.label: Strozzapreti
children.fact: Means "priest stranglers" — legend says local women made this pasta for the clergy as payment, and the priests ate so greedily they choked on it.

children.label: Casarecce
children.fact: Each piece is a small sheet rolled into a loose S-scroll. The name means "homemade" — it was originally a pasta made only at home, never commercially produced.

children.label: Busiate
children.fact: From western Sicily, each spiral is rolled around a thin rod or reed called a busa, the same tool that gave the pasta its name.

children.label: Fileja
children.fact: A Calabrian pasta rolled around a thin metal rod called a dinaculu, creating a hollow center without any extrusion at all.

children.label: Gemelli
children.fact: They look like two strands twisted together, but are usually a single folded rope.

children.label: Radiatori
children.fact: It was inspired by industrial radiator fins in the twentieth century.

children.label: Malloreddus
children.fact: Known as gnocchetti sardi, these striped Sardinian shells were traditionally rolled over wicker baskets and often tinted yellow with saffron.

children.label: Stelline
children.fact: For many Italians, this is the first pasta they ever eat in soup.

children.label: Anelli
children.fact: The tiny rings are a classic in Sicilian baked timballo.

children.label: Anellini
children.fact: It is the smaller ring shape most often packed into brothy soups.

children.label: Acini di pepe
children.fact: Its name means peppercorns, even though the bits look more like couscous.

children.label: Orzo
children.fact: The name means barley, but it is entirely wheat pasta.

children.label: Pastina
children.fact: Pastina is both a shape family and a comfort-food category.

children.label: Fregola
children.fact: One of the few Italian pastas intentionally toasted before cooking, these Sardinian semolina beads keep a nutty flavor even after simmering in broth.

children.label: Conchigliette
children.fact: The shell cup is perfect for catching broth and grated cheese.

children.label: Ditalini
children.fact: Its name means little thimbles, which is exactly the silhouette.

children.label: Tortellini
children.fact: Legend says the shape was inspired by Venus's navel.

children.label: Tortelloni
children.fact: It is larger than tortellini and usually filled with softer, meatless fillings.

children.label: Cappelletti
children.fact: Its name means little hats, and the folded brim is easy to spot.

children.label: Cappellacci
children.fact: Means "big ugly hats" — a larger, more rustic version of cappelletti from Ferrara. Traditionally filled with pumpkin and amaretti biscuits, a combination that sounds wrong and tastes extraordinary.

children.label: Agnolotti del plin
children.fact: "Plin" means "pinch" in Piedmontese dialect — each tiny parcel is sealed with a single pinch of the fingers. Traditionally filled with leftover roast meat, making it a pasta born from frugality.

children.label: Ravioli
children.fact: The crimped edges were as much about sealing as decoration.

children.label: Agnolotti
children.fact: In Piedmont, leftover roast meat often became the filling.

children.label: Culurgiones
children.fact: A Sardinian stuffed pasta sealed with an elaborate braided edge that looks like a wheat stalk. The folding technique is so specific that each village in Ogliastra has its own variation, and locals can identify which village made it by the braid pattern.

children.label: Schlutzkrapfen
children.fact: A half-moon pasta from South Tyrol, where Italian and Austrian traditions meet — the dough uses rye flour and the filling is spinach and ricotta. It sits on the border between pasta and dumpling, and locals debate which it is.

children.label: Pansotti
children.fact: These Ligurian stuffed triangles are traditionally filled with wild preboggion greens and dressed with walnut sauce, not tomato or meat ragù.

children.label: Sacchettini
children.fact: The top is pinched into a tiny purse shape after filling.

children.label: Cannelloni
children.fact: These large tubes are usually filled first and baked second.

children.label: What kind of hand-shape is it?
Orecchiette
children.fact: Means "little ears." In Bari, it is still made by street vendors who sit outside their homes dragging small rounds of dough across wooden boards with a butter knife — a technique passed from mother to daughter for generations.

children.label: Cavatelli
children.fact: Made by pressing a finger along a small piece of dough and dragging it to create a curl — one of the oldest pasta-making gestures, essentially unchanged since the Middle Ages.

children.label: Cencioni
children.fact: Means "little rags" — small irregular petal shapes from Tuscany, pressed with a thumb to create a curved, rough surface. Each piece looks slightly different from the last.

children.label: Maltagliati
children.fact: The name means "badly cut" — these are intentionally irregular triangles torn or cut from pasta sheets without any uniform shape. Imperfection is the entire aesthetic.

children.label: Sagne 'mpastrate
children.fact: A Calabrian pasta of hand-torn ribbons deliberately made uneven. The rough edges catch thick vegetable sauces in ways a clean-cut pasta cannot — the irregularity is functional, not accidental.

children.label: Lorighittas
children.fact: A Sardinian pasta made by twisting two strands together into a ring, then braiding the join. Traditionally made only on All Saints' Day — each ring takes about a minute to form by hand.

children.label: Corzetti
children.fact: These coin-like rounds from Liguria are pressed with carved wooden stamps, and older molds often carried aristocratic family crests or symbolic patterns.

children.label: What is it made or shaped like?
Gnocchi
children.fact: Many Italians will happily argue all night about whether it counts as pasta.

children.label: Gnudi
children.fact: The name means naked because it is ravioli filling without the wrapper.
